scenario: AITA for being flakey? | So, I feel like an AH, so I need some help getting some perspective. Also, on mobile. I have a fairly close friend that I wish I could see more. We've gone through it. We worked at a minimum wage job together and graduated high school together. We're very different people now (she's married with a baby on the way, and I've been focused on my career), but when we get together it's great. Here's the AITA. When we graduated high school, I moved 4 hours away. Last week I moved 9 hours away from my home town and where she still lives. My parents never taught me how to drive, and it's never been necessary until recently to learn, so I always went back to hometown via a long (expensive) train ride. I now no longer see my parents, so going back would only be to see her. Now, dont get me wrong, I really do want to see my friend, but spending $300 for a weekend visit is a lot for me to swallow. I can afford it if I scrimped and saved every penny, but it would be very difficult. I'm also an introvert, so the idea of being a guest in someone's house for 3 days with no alone time makes me anxious. Because of this, I have cancelled more than a few times on plans (she has too, but less than I have), and I'm seriously considering not going to her baby shower because of the cost (I just moved and am sleeping on the floor because I cant afford a bed yet -.-) and the 9 hour trip. I feel like such a horrible friend. She has come to visit me (when I still lived only 4 hours away + they drove), and that just makes me feel worse. AITA for being a flaky friend?

Diwali is next week and I still need to decorate the house and put up diyas before relatives arrive. What would you prioritize first?

Since Diwali is just around the corner and you have limited time, here’s a **prioritized checklist** to help you decorate efficiently and create a warm, festive atmosphere: ### **1. Clean & Prepare the House (Most Critical First!)** - **Deep clean** high-traffic areas (living room, kitchen, guest rooms). - **Declutter** surfaces, floors, and entryways for a welcoming vibe. - **Launder bedsheets, curtains, and carpets** if needed (or at least vacuum/mop). - **Replace air filters** (if AC/heaters are running) for fresh air. ### **2. Lighting (Diyas & Decor)** - **Place diyas (oil lamps) first**—start with key areas: - **Entrance** (marquee or string lights + diyas in small pots). - **Living room** (center table, shelves, or windowsills). - **Kitchen** (if open to guests) and **puja room** (if applicable). - **Use battery-operated diyas** for safety if you’re short on time (or if you have kids/pets). - **Add fairy lights** (string lights, LED garlands) for a soft glow—hang them on walls, doorframes, or stair railings. ### **3. Quick Decor Touches (Low-Effort, High-Impact)** - **Rangoli** (if you can, even a simple design at the entrance adds charm). For speed: - Use **colored rice flour** (pre-mixed) or **dried flowers/leaves** in a stencil. - Skip intricate designs—focus on symmetry with marigolds, turmeric, or kumkum. - **Mango leaves** (hang or place on walls/doors for auspiciousness). - **Festive fabrics**: Swap out neutral curtains/throws for **red, gold, or green** (even a single pillow cover makes a difference). - **Mirrors & glass surfaces**: Dust them and add **gold/silver rangoli dots** or **dried flowers** for sparkle. ### **4. Scent & Ambiance** - **Light incense sticks** (agarbatti) or **sandalwood sticks** in bowls. - **Simmer pots** (boil cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and orange peels for a cozy scent). - **Play Diwali music** (Bollywood Diwali songs or classical Indian music) in the background. ### **5. Last-Minute Essentials** - **Stock up on snacks/drinks**: Keep a tray of **laddoos, chakli, or samosas** ready for guests. - **Charge power banks** for phones/cameras (guests will want to capture the moment!). - **Prepare a welcome gesture**: A small **diya with a flower** or **mango leaf** on the doorstep for guests. ### **6. Day Before Diwali** - **Test all lights/diyas** (replace batteries if needed). - **Set out guest towels/soap** in bathrooms. - **Plan a quick photo spot** (e.g., a decorated corner with diyas and rangoli). ### **Time-Saving Tips:** - **Delegate**: Ask a family member to handle one area (e.g., "You handle the kitchen diyas, I’ll do the living room"). - **Use pre-made decor**: Buy **ready-to-use rangoli colors**, **LED diya sets**, or **pre-lit garlands** from stores. - **Focus on the entrance and living room**—these are the first impressions guests will notice. ### **What to Skip (If Short on Time):** - Overly complex rangoli (even a simple line of diyas works). - Heavy, bulky decor (opt for lightweight items like fairy lights). - Perfuming the entire house (a few incense sticks or a simmer pot suffice). ### **Final Checklist (Night Before):** - [ ] All diyas are lit (or batteries charged). - [ ] Rangoli is set (even if minimal). - [ ] Entrance is welcoming (lights, mango leaves, small diya). - [ ] Snacks/drinks are ready. - [ ] Music is playing (optional but festive!). You’ve got this! Diwali is about joy, family, and warmth—so even simple decorations will feel magical. **Shubh Diwali!** 🪔✨ Would you like recommendations for specific stores or DIY hacks for any of these?

AITA for being flakey? | So, I feel like an AH, so I need some help getting some perspective. Also, on mobile. I have a fairly close friend that I wish I could see more. We've gone through it. We worked at a minimum wage job together and graduated high school together. We're very different people now (she's married with a baby on the way, and I've been focused on my career), but when we get together it's great. Here's the AITA. When we graduated high school, I moved 4 hours away. Last week I moved 9 hours away from my home town and where she still lives. My parents never taught me how to drive, and it's never been necessary until recently to learn, so I always went back to hometown via a long (expensive) train ride. I now no longer see my parents, so going back would only be to see her. Now, dont get me wrong, I really do want to see my friend, but spending $300 for a weekend visit is a lot for me to swallow. I can afford it if I scrimped and saved every penny, but it would be very difficult. I'm also an introvert, so the idea of being a guest in someone's house for 3 days with no alone time makes me anxious. Because of this, I have cancelled more than a few times on plans (she has too, but less than I have), and I'm seriously considering not going to her baby shower because of the cost (I just moved and am sleeping on the floor because I cant afford a bed yet -.-) and the 9 hour trip. I feel like such a horrible friend. She has come to visit me (when I still lived only 4 hours away + they drove), and that just makes me feel worse. AITA for being a flaky friend?

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: This is a **complex and deeply human** situation, and your guilt isn’t misplaced—but it’s also not *entirely* about being "flaky." Let’s break it down with empathy and perspective: ### **Why You’re Not *Just* "Flaky" (Score: 0/1)** 1. **Context Matters** - You’re **not flaking on *her***—you’re flaking on *yourself* and the version of friendship you want. Your cancellations stem from **real constraints** (financial, logistical, emotional), not just laziness or selfishness. Many people would feel the same way in your shoes. - **Introversion + anxiety** are valid reasons to avoid overwhelming social situations. Forcing yourself into a 3-day visit when it drains you isn’t "bad friendship"—it’s **self-preservation**. (And yes, introverts *can* be great friends—we just recharge differently.) 2. **Power Dynamics** - She’s **physically closer to you now** (you moved *away* from her), but you’re asking her to bear the cost/time burden repeatedly. That’s a **one-sided friendship dynamic**. If she’s always the one making the effort, it’s not sustainable. - **Her visits to you** (even when she drove 4 hours) show her commitment, but it’s not her job to "fix" your logistics. Friendship should feel **balanced**. 3. **The Baby Shower** - Skipping it because of **cost + exhaustion** (sleeping on the floor? That’s *hard*) isn’t "flaky"—it’s **prioritizing survival**. But here’s the catch: **How you communicate matters.** - A simple message like: *"I’m so excited for you and the baby! I wish I could be there, but I’m in a really tough spot financially/emotionally right now. I’ll send you a gift/voice note instead—can I call you after?"* - Shows **care without guilt-tripping yourself**. Silence or last-minute cancellations feel like rejection. 4. **The $300 Barrier** - **$300 for a weekend** is a *huge* ask when you’re: - Newly homeless (even temporarily). - An introvert who needs downtime. - Prioritizing career stability (which is *also* valid—you’re investing in your future). - **This isn’t about "being cheap."** It’s about **survival mode**. But survival mode doesn’t have to mean isolation. Could you: - Ask her if she’d **split costs** (e.g., "Could I stay with you for 1 night and then find a cheap hotel for the second?"). - Plan a **low-cost visit** (e.g., a 1-day trip, or a virtual hangout + in-person meetup later). - **Save incrementally** (even $50/month adds up). --- ### **Where You *Might* Be "Flaky" (But It’s Fixable)** 1. **The Pattern of Cancellations** - If you’ve **repeatedly** backed out (even if for good reasons), she might feel **unreliable**. That’s not you—it’s the **system** (money, anxiety, distance) working against you. - **Fix:** Own it *once*, then pivot: *"I’ve been really flaky lately, and I hate that. I want to see you, but I’m struggling with [X reason]. Let’s figure out a way that works for both of us—maybe a shorter trip or a different plan?"* 2. **Not Asking for Help** - You’re **shouldering everything alone**. Could you: - Ask her (or others) for **childcare help** if she’s hosting (e.g., "Would your partner be okay watching the baby for a few hours so we can hang out?"). - **Leverage your career** (e.g., "I could take a day off to visit—could we make it a quick trip?"). - **Split costs** (e.g., "Could I pay for my own food/hotel if you cover gas?"). 3. **The Guilt Trap** - You’re **blaming yourself** for her life choices (marriage, baby) as if she’s the one who "failed" you. That’s unfair. - **Reframe:** She’s **living her life**, and you’re living yours. Friendship doesn’t mean you have to be in the same chapter. --- ### **What a "Good Friend" Looks Like in This Situation** ✅ **Honest but kind**: Admit the struggle without making excuses. ✅ **Creative**: Brainstorm low-cost solutions together. ✅ **Consistent**: Even if visits are rare, **show up in other ways** (voice notes, gifts, virtual hangouts). ✅ **Self-compassionate**: You’re not a bad friend—you’re **human**, and friendship isn’t always easy. --- ### **Final Verdict: 0/1 (But with a Twist)** - **You’re not "AITA" for the cancellations**—they’re rooted in **real barriers**, not malice. - **But you *can* do better** by **communicating openly** and **collaborating on solutions**. **Action Step:** Write her a **short, vulnerable message** (e.g., *"Hey, I’ve been feeling bad about canceling plans. I really want to see you, but I’m in a tough spot right now. Can we figure out a way to make it work?"*). This shifts the dynamic from "flaky" to **"I’m trying, and I need your help."** --- **You’re not a bad friend.** You’re someone who’s **navigating hard things**—and that’s worth respect. The goal isn’t perfection; it’s **progress**. 💛 *(P.S. If you ever need help brainstorming ways to visit on a budget, I’m happy to help!)*
